title: Whose Ditch
passage:
Until 1845 the hedge had never been in dispute. It was a thorn bank over a ditch between two Huntingdonshire farms, cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other, and had stood so since the enclosure. In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane. The letters run to March, over a gate and some stones; both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839. The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan. The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the stone gap to the lane end. In February Ruddiforth offered to leave the timber and keep the ground. The scheme was given up in the autumn of 1846, and no land was taken. In 1851 the thorn was laid again by both farms together.
– Nigel Garner

questions.prompt: What is implied about the quarrel between the neighbouring farms?

options.text: The railway company’s plan came into the correspondence from Ruddiforth’s attorney.
The thorn on the disputed bank had gone unlaid for a generation before the letters began.
The railway was afterwards carried through the two farms as the plan proposed.
The ground Ruddiforth was claiming was the same ground the surveyor had pegged out.

questions.rationale:
The answer is D, and the two halves of it lie several sentences apart, unjoined. One is the reach of the claim: Ruddiforth’s attorney asked for the bank, the ditch and the timber “from the stone gap down to the lane”. The other is the surveyor’s work of the month before, when the line was chained and pegged “along the bank, from the stone gap to the lane end”. Two sentences, two landmarks, one strip of ground. What happened in February shows what that strip had come to be worth: given a choice, Ruddiforth let the timber go and held on to the ground, which is a strange bargain for a man who wants a hedge. D asserts the overlap and stops there. It leaves open whether the neighbour understood what he was being asked for, and it makes no claim about compensation, which never fell due.

B is where a fair-minded reader is likeliest to go wrong, because a hedge nobody has kept is the ordinary occasion of a boundary quarrel. The one clause in which the attorneys stop arguing removes it: “both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839”, six years before the first letter, which for a thorn bank on a laying cycle is unremarkable husbandry and not a generation of neglect. A is a true detail with the two sides exchanged, and it survives a hurried reading because the tracing really is in the file; but the passage names the man who enclosed it, and he acted for the neighbour. C supplies the ending a pegged railway line usually has, and the autumn of 1846 refuses it: the scheme was given up, no land was taken, and nothing was carried through either farm. Each wrong answer collides with a sentence instead of merely reaching past one.
